# On learning disentangled representations for individual treatment effect estimation

Author links open overlay panel Jiebin Chu ^{a}, Zhoujian Sun ^{a}, Wei Dong ^{b}, Jinlong Shi ^{c}, Zhengxing Huang ^{a}

## Highlights

  * •

To alleviate the problem of selection bias in individualized treatment effect estimation.

  * •

To disentangle outcome-oriented and treatment-oriented factors from input patient features by using representation learning.

  * •

To employ an individualized orthogonal regularization to eliminate confounders in the latent representations.

  * •

Evaluation is done using a semi-simulated dataset and a real-world dataset for the task of individualized treatment effect estimation.

## Abstract

### Objective

Estimating the individualized treatment effect (ITE) from observational data is a challenging task due to selection bias, which results from the distributional discrepancy between different treatment groups caused by the dependence between features and assigned treatments. This dependence is induced by the factors related to the treatment assignment. We hypothesize that features consist of three types of latent factors: outcome-specific factors, treatment-specific factors and confounders. Then, we aim to reduce the influence of treatment-related factors, i.e., treatment-specific factors and confounders, on outcome prediction to mitigate the effects of selection bias.

### Method

We present a novel representation learning model in which both the main task of outcome prediction and the auxiliary task of classifying the treatment assignment are used to learn the outcome-oriented and treatment-oriented latent representations, respectively. However, since the confounders are related to both treatment assignment and outcome, it is still contained in the representations. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Abstract

We study matching queues with abandonment. The simplest of these is the two-sided queue with servers on one side and customers on the other, both arriving dynamically over time and abandoning if not matched by the time their patience elapses. We identify nonasymptotic and universal scaling laws for the matching loss due to abandonment, which we refer to as the “cost of impatience.” We prove that the ability to hold inventory of servers means that the optimal safety capacity grows logarithmically in abandonment cost and, in turn, slower than the square-root growth in the single-sided queue.

# Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments

Siqi He, Yehua Wei, Jiaming Xu

November 1, 2026·math.OC·arXiv:2611.01431

## Abstract

We study a dynamic two-way matching market in which agents of heterogeneous types arrive over time, wait to be matched according to a compatibility network, and abandon the system if their random patience expires. The decision maker collects match rewards and pays holding and abandonment costs, and seeks to maximize the expected net value over a finite horizon. We evaluate policies by their approximation ratio against a fluid benchmark, the optimal value of a linear-programming relaxation that upper bounds the expected net value of every policy. Under a general position gap (GPG) condition, which requires the unique optimal dual solution of this linear program to remain optimal under small perturbations of the arrival rates, we propose a longest-queue policy. The policy first uses this dual solution to identify a set of good match types and a set of critical agent types. Upon each arrival, it considers only good matches and matches the arrival to the critical partner with the longest queue subject to availabilities. In the high-volume regime, in which arrival rates are scaled by s, we prove that the policy attains an approximation ratio of at least 1-O(1/s) at every scale s >= 1 and every horizon T >= 1, so the ratio tends to 1 as s goes to infinity.

## Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming finance through rapid technological innovation. Early applications in financial institutions primarily focused on language-oriented tasks such as translation, document summarization, and conversational interfaces, improving operational efficiency and access to information. More recently, however, AI has begun to play a direct role in financial decision-making, influencing portfolio construction, trading, risk management, and execution. In this context, decision-focused learning has emerged as a powerful end-to-end paradigm that trains predictive models directly for downstream decision quality rather than intermediate prediction accuracy. Departing from the traditional predict-then-optimize framework, decision-focused learning integrates prediction and optimization by defining learning objectives in terms of realized economic or risk-based outcomes. This study surveys the growing use of decision-focused learning in financial research, including applications in portfolio construction and risk management. We find that recent developments suggest decision-focused learning offers a promising framework for aligning machine learning with financial decision-making, while raising open questions regarding robustness, transparency, and economic interpretability.

Title: Poisson Super Learning For Survival And Competing Risks On A Discretized Time Scale
Authors: Gabriele Pittarello, Thomas Gerds, Pernille Falberg Rønn, Helene Charlotte Rytgaard
Date: Mon Nov  2 15:03:00 2026

We introduce the Poisson Super Learner, a scalable ensemble method for survival and competing risks prediction with right-censored data. The approach exploits the correspondence between the likelihood of piecewise-constant hazard models and the Poisson likelihood. After expanding the data over a chosen time partition, candidate hazard learners are trained under a common Poisson loss, and cross-validated log-hazard predictions are combined by a Poisson meta learner. The resulting ensemble is a geometric combination of candidate hazards, and can be used to estimate survival probabilities and cause-specific absolute risks. The Poisson Super Learner framework is modular and can in principle incorporate any learner that can estimate interval-specific hazards, including parametric, penalised, additive, and other machine-learning hazard models. Training targets the cause-specific hazard directly and does not require explicit modelling of the censoring distribution. For competing risks, separate cause-specific ensembles are fitted and subsequently combined to obtain individualised cumulative incidence predictions. We illustrate the approach using data from the Steno Diabetes Center collected between 2005 and 2022 to predict cardiovascular disease risk in patients with type 1 diabetes from detailed covariate information. The applied analysis is complemented by simulation studies designed to reflect key features of the data and to examine the behaviour of the method under controlled settings. In the online Minimum cost Bipartite Perfect Matching with Delays (MBPMD) problem, $m$ requests and $m$ servers arrive over time in a metric space. On the line, Kuo proposed the Virtual Robust Matching (VRM) algorithm and showed that it is $O(\sqrt{m}\log^2 m)$-competitive. We prove that VRM is $O(\log m)$-competitive for the MBPMD problem in any metric space. VRM is deterministic and does not need to know the metric space or $m$ in advance. It is the first deterministic polylogarithmic-competitive algorithm for the MBPMD problem in general metric spaces. Unlike the previous analysis of VRM, our analysis does not rely on a geometric decomposition of the metric space. Instead, it charges the waiting time of requests over time to the edges of a fixed optimal matching. We also extend VRM to the non-bipartite version and prove that the resulting deterministic algorithm is $O(\log m)$-competitive. Individuals are heterogeneous, so are their responses to treatments or programs. One complication in measuring AI’s effect on productivity is that it has different effects on different tasks, and this causes people to change how they allocate their time between tasks. This makes it more difficult to talk about the effect of AI on overall productivity.

# Parsimonious Learning-Augmented Online Metric Matching

Yongho Shin, Phanu Vajanopath

ICML 2026 3

## Introduction

Online metric matching is a classic optimization problem: given $n$n servers at fixed locations, $n$n requests appear sequentially. Each request must be immediately and irrevocably matched to an available server to minimize the total distance traveled. Standard algorithms often take a pessimistic approach, assuming worst-case future scenarios, which results in a competitive ratio of $2n-1$2 n−1.

Recent advancements in "learning-augmented" algorithms suggest that using machine learning to predict future requests can drastically improve performance. However, generating these predictions at every step is often computationally prohibitive. This paper explores a practical middle ground: What if we can only afford to query a prediction every $k$k steps? The authors introduce a "parsimonious" framework that maintains high performance (consistency) when predictions are accurate, while ensuring the algorithm doesn't fail catastrophically (robustness) if the predictions are flawed.

## The Parsimonious Framework and Virtual Predictions

The authors propose a meta-algorithm based on the Follow-the-Prediction (FtP) framework. Because traditional FtP requires a prediction at every single time step, the authors developed a novel method to fill the "silence" between actual predictions spaced $k$k steps apart.

They achieve this through Virtual Predictions. During the gaps between actual predictions, the algorithm runs a standard, prediction-free online matching algorithm on the "residual" servers and requests. The output of this sub-algorithm serves as a virtual prediction to keep the FtP framework running smoothly.

For this approach to succeed, the underlying sub-algorithm must possess two critical properties:

  1. Adherence: The algorithm must maintain a good matching at every intermediate step, staying close to the optimal matching of the requests seen so far.
  2. Strong Competitiveness: It must reliably perform well even without future knowledge.

To handle noisy or incorrect predictions, the authors implement a "Combination Algorithm." 
## Empirical Evaluation

The framework was evaluated across three types of instances:

  * Line: A 1D metric space with 200 vertices.
  * Plane: A 2D metric space using Euclidean distance.
  * Taxi (Real-world): Derived from the Chicago Taxi Trips (2013–2023) dataset, using recent drop-off locations as servers and upcoming pick-up locations as requests (measured via Manhattan distance).

In the Chicago Taxi experiments, the parsimonious algorithm consistently outperformed standard greedy and competitive baselines. Remarkably, even with a large prediction gap ($k=20$k=20), the algorithm maintained significantly better solution quality than prediction-free alternatives. The experiments also revealed an interesting dynamic regarding noise sensitivity: the algorithm is more sensitive to prediction noise when $k$k is small (frequent predictions) but becomes more stable as $k$k increases, albeit with a higher baseline cost.

## Limitations and Future Directions

While highly effective, the framework has a few limitations that pave the way for future research:

  * The "Robustness Tax": The Combination Algorithm incurs a multiplicative overhead factor of 9 to guarantee robustness. In practice, when the performance gap is narrow, this overhead can sometimes cause the combined algorithm to underperform compared to a simple greedy approach.
  * Randomized Querying: The current lower bounds assume a deterministic schedule for querying the oracle. Exploring randomized query schedules could unlock even better performance guarantees.
  * Alternative Prediction Models: Future work could investigate different ways to model prediction error, such as "outlier" models where the vast majority of predictions are perfect, but a few are entirely incorrect.

By bridging the gap between traditional online algorithms and full-knowledge models, this parsimonious approach offers a highly practical blueprint for deploying learning-augmented algorithms in computationally constrained environments.
